title: Pavarana again
hook: invite honest feedback at the end of the rains

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ullambana, and a gift for one mother given through many people. Your line was for the ancestors. Whose name did you carry with you? Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

"Be honest. Tear it apart." A friend hands you a draft, a business plan, a wedding speech. So you're honest. You point out the slow middle and the joke that doesn't land. And you watch their face close like a door. They asked for it, and they didn't want it. Asking is the easy part. Hearing is hard. At the end of the rains retreat, monks gather for a ceremony called Pavarana, the invitation, and each one asks the others to name his faults. You've met it before. This time, look less at the asking and more at the second half: what the one who asks is promising to do with the answer.
screen: `BE HONEST. TEAR IT APART.` → `ASKING IS EASY.` → `HEARING IS HARD.`

segments.voice: First, the words. In the monastic rule, each monk, in turn, invites the community: if you've seen anything, or heard anything, or even suspected anything, speak to me out of compassion, and seeing it, I will make amends. Notice the three doors he opens. Seen, heard, suspected. He's not only asking about what's been proven. He's letting people bring a worry. Second, the reason they're allowed to speak: out of compassion. Not to win. Not to score a point after a season together. The invitation sets the tone for the answer. Third, the promise at the end. Seeing it, I will make amends. That's the part the friend with the wedding speech forgot. The one who asks isn't just bracing to be hurt. He's agreeing ahead of time to look, and to fix what he finds. Fourth, why it's needed. The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's words: "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive." The verse is plain about blind spots. Another verse goes further, and calls the person who points out your faults someone who shows you where treasure is. In paraphrase: if you find a wise person who reproves you, stay close to them, the way you'd follow someone who knows where gold is buried. It will be better for you, not worse. So Pavarana isn't a punishment at the end of the rains. It's a community lending each other their eyes.
screen: `SEEN, HEARD, SUSPECTED.` · `SPEAK OUT OF COMPASSION.` · `SEEING IT, I WILL MAKE AMENDS.` · then, large: `TELL ME MY FAULTS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one person who knows you well and wishes you well: a friend, a partner, a colleague, a sibling. Picture asking them, gently: is there one thing I do that's hard to be around? Notice what happens in your body at the thought. Maybe the shoulders lift. Maybe the jaw tightens. Just notice. Now picture hearing their answer, whatever it is, and saying back: thank you; I'll look at that. Let the breath stay slow. Rest there, with the open door, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pavarana. The invitation at the end of the rains, when each monk asks the others to name his faults, and promises to make amends. Today's word.
Your line: tell me my faults. Today, ask one person you trust for one honest word, and whatever it is, answer only: thank you. Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: At the end of the rains retreat, Theravada monks gather on the full moon for Pavarana, and each in turn invites the community to point out any fault seen, heard or suspected; lay people often bring offerings to the temple that day.

pairs: like one who shows buried treasure

myth: in the invitation, a monk asks only about faults that have been proven
he asks about anything seen, heard, or even suspected.
the one who asks promises to make amends for what he's shown
the words end: seeing it, I will make amends.
the Dhammapada says our own faults are easy to see
it says the faults of others are easily perceived, and our own are difficult to perceive.

fork.setup: you asked a friend to name a fault. they name one, and it stings. what does the Pavarana formula have you say?
options: seeing it, I will make amends.
fork.reveal: the one who invites promises ahead of time: seeing it, I will make amends.

original.note: Pali pavarana: the invitation, made at the end of the rains retreat.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pavarana is a confession ceremony.
what it means: an invitation to others to name your faults, out of compassion, with a promise to make amends.
what a scholar hears: the Vinaya's formula of seen, heard and suspected, and Dhammapada 76's reprover who points to treasure.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 4 (Pavaranakkhandhaka), the formula of invitation

sources.quoted: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive

notes: Mahavagga 4 formula paraphrased: 'I invite the Sangha in regard to what has been seen, heard or suspected; let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion; seeing it, I will make amends.' Confirm.
Dhammapada 252 quoted from Müller (1881); confirm wording.
Dhammapada 76 paraphrased (the wise man who administers reproofs as one who points out hidden treasure; 'better, not worse'). Confirm the paraphrase is close.
Earlier Pavarana days (y2 688, y3 1045) used the silent-monks story and the Buddha's own invitation (SN 8.7); this day focuses on the receiving half of the formula.
